source_text: Verum consignata hac disputationis summa prudentis animo lectoris, excutiamus quid Baptisma tuum, quod propter solam genitalium commotionem dicis fuisse provisum, crediti sibi muneris exsequatur. Profitetur se a peccatis homines expiare, sed cum apud iustitiam causa agitur voluntatis, non pronuntiatur rea, quae aliud velle non potuit. Evanescente autem invidia reatus, etiam pompa indulgentis evanuit; quia non potest ignoscere, quod iure non potest imputare. Ac per hoc, promissionis suae frustratur effectibus; quoniam nec invenit crimina, quorum remissione laudetur; nec habet huius beneficii debitores, quo peccatorum vincula solvuntur; quia in necessitatis asylo collocatos non potest malae convincere voluntatis; per quae omnia supervacuum de ehenditur. Verum quia gratia quae a Christo provisa est, supervacua non est; rationabilis eius munificentia teneatur, per quod rea voluntas convincitur peccatoris, quae potuit utique tam bonum velle, quam malum voluit. Totum ergo figmentum necessitatis evanuit; ac per hoc, nullum est de naturae conditione peccatum; sed liberum arbitrium in natura hominum perseverat; quod ut tu cum Manichaeis negas, ita nos cum Apostolis et omnibus Catholicis confitemur.
pass_a_gloss: But this sum of the disputation having been sealed in the mind of a prudent reader, let us shake out what your Baptism, which you say was provided on account of the stirring of the genitals alone, carries out of the gift entrusted to it. It professes that it expiates humans from sins, but when before justice the cause of will is driven, she is not pronounced guilty, who could not will another thing. But with the ill-will of guilt vanishing, the pomp also of the one indulging has vanished; because he cannot pardon, what he cannot by right impute. And through this, he is frustrated of the effects of his own promise; since he neither finds crimes, by whose remission he may be praised; nor has debtors of this benefit, by which the bonds of sins are loosed; because he cannot convict those placed in the asylum of necessity of an evil will; through all which things it is caught superfluous. But because the grace which has been provided by Christ is not superfluous; let its reasonable munificence be held, through which the guilty will of the sinner is convicted, which could at any rate will good as much as it willed evil. The whole fiction therefore of necessity has vanished; and through this, there is no sin from the condition of nature; but free choice perseveres in the nature of humans; which as you deny with the Manichaeans, so we confess with the Apostles and all Catholics.

lemmas.lexica: LS/Blaise natura=created constitution, not 'original sin' itself
LS peccatum=fault, error; Blaise Christian sin
LS voluntas=will, wish; Blaise moral will
LS arbitrium=judgment, free decision; Blaise liberum arbitrium
LS liber=free; Blaise unde liberum est abstinere

pass_b_english: With this conclusion of our discussion sealed in the sensible reader's mind, let us examine how your baptism, which you say was provided solely because of the stirring of the genitals, performs its entrusted task. It professes to cleanse human beings from sins. But when the will's case is heard before justice, a will that could not will otherwise is not pronounced guilty. When the accusation of guilt vanishes, the display of pardon vanishes too: one cannot forgive what one cannot rightly impute. Thus it fails to fulfill its promise. It finds no crimes whose forgiveness might earn it praise, nor anyone indebted to it for the benefit by which the bonds of sins are loosed, because it cannot convict those sheltered in the sanctuary of necessity of an evil will. All this shows it to be superfluous.

But the grace provided by Christ is not superfluous. Let us retain a rational account of its generosity, by which the sinner's will is proved guilty, since it could certainly have willed good just as it willed evil. The entire fiction of necessity therefore vanishes. Consequently, there is no sin from the condition of nature; free choice remains in human nature. You deny it with the Manichaeans; we acknowledge it with the apostles and all catholics.

choices.why: Julian's charge against Augustine: treating evil as a nature rather than as will.
Julian's forensic/moral fault tied to will, not a substance in nature.

anf_compare.notes: Victorian English of some of Julian survives inside NPNF Augustine (chiefly On Marriage and Concupiscence and related anti-Pelagian books). NPNF was not copied. Pass A is a literal gloss of Augustinus.it Latin of Julian's words only; Augustine's replies in the same locus are excluded.

speaker: Julian of Eclanum (words preserved in Augustine, Opus imperfectum contra Iulianum); Augustine's reply at this locus is excluded.
